chapters.title: The Far Side of the Table

spans.text: This is the second book in a series called The American Firsts, and I want to say at the start that I do not like the name and that the discomfort is the point.

A first is a thing you win. It is the word for a record, an achievement, a flag on a hill. We have attached it, over about a century, to a category of American event that nobody competed for and nobody survived on purpose, and we have done it because the alternative is to admit that these things are not a series at all, that they have no shape, and that the only reason we can put them in an order is that we have had enough of them to make a list.
So the series is named for the habit rather than for the events, and each book is an argument with its own title.

The event in this one took about twelve minutes on the morning of Tuesday, 6 September 1949, on one block of one street in East Camden, New Jersey. Thirteen people were killed and three were wounded. It is generally described now as the first mass shooting of its kind in modern America, by which people mean one man on foot with a pistol going door to door through an ordinary commercial street in the middle of a working morning, and I have come to think that description is close enough to true to be worth arguing with and not close enough to be worth repeating.
There were massacres before it. What was new was the form, and the form is why the word stuck.
What this book is about
It is not about him.

I decided that before I wrote a word and I have not broken it. He is never given a point of view, not for a line, not anywhere in this book. He is seen from outside, heard through a wall, quoted from the public record, and written about by people who are frightened of him or who have not noticed him. His name appears three times in sixty-eight chapters. He is never explained, because I do not think anybody knows and I am certain that I do not, and because a novel that explains him would be doing the one thing this whole form does badly and does constantly.
The book is about the block.

Roughly two thirds of it takes place before anything happens. Thirty-four chapters, two years, one street of about forty households, in the most prosperous decade that street would ever have. A barber, a shoemaker, a druggist on the corner, a tailor at the far end, a man on the eleven to seven at the radio works, women doing the wash on a Monday because that is the day the wash was done. Nobody in those chapters knows what is coming, and none of them is a symbol, and none of their ordinary days is arranged so as to be poignant later.
That is a considerable demand to make of a reader and I want to be straight about why I am making it.
The bargain
You know what happens. You knew before you opened this book, and if you did not, the back cover told you.

That is not a flaw in a book like this. It is the only working engine it has. Every one of those thirty-four chapters is read twice at once: once as what it is, which is a Tuesday, and once as what you know it to be, which is the second to last Tuesday. The people in them get no such double reading. They get the Tuesday.

Everything in this book is built on that gap. It is why the first part is long. It is why nothing in it is ominous. It is why, when the shooting comes, it is not described from anywhere useful, and no character in it understands what they are hearing, and nobody gets a good view.
I have tried very hard not to give you a good view.
What I owe you
Three things, and I would rather put them here than let you find them out at the back.

The dead in this book are real and are named. All thirteen of them, and the three who were wounded and lived. Nobody who dies in these pages was invented. Their names, ages, trades and addresses come from the record.

Everything those people think and feel is mine. The record gives a name, an age, a trade and an address and gives nothing else at all. A six-year-old boy in this book has a loose tooth and a bargain with a milkman about it. No source records that, or anything else, about what any of these people were like. I have invented the insides of real dead people, and I have done it carefully, and it is still an invention.

The rest of the street is made up. Every neighbour who carries a name here is a composite under a name I invented, because the people who lived on that block had children and those children had children and a great many of them are alive.

There is a fuller accounting at the back, in the Author's Note, and an appendix after it setting out what the record actually contains for each of the sixteen and where I got it. If you are the sort of reader who checks, and I hope you are, start there and come back.
One last thing, and it is the fact that reorganised this book after I thought I had it planned.

Of the thirteen people who died on that block, six were not from it. One was collecting insurance. One was driving through. One was a child who had been brought there for a haircut. Three of them were stopped at a traffic light in a car.
The premise of this book is a man who kept a list of his neighbours.
Fewer than half the people he killed were his neighbours.
J. L. C.
River Rd. what they have done.
The shoes came in worse than people thought they were and went out better than people expected, and that gap was the whole of the business.

John Pilarchik came over the bridge from Pennsauken on the seven-forty bus with his jacket over his arm because it was already too warm for it, and he got down at the corner of Thirty-second and walked the half block to his own door the way he had walked it for four years, which is to say without looking at anything. A man does not look at the street he works on. He looks at the lock, and at the mat, and at whether the boy from the bakery has left the crate where he was asked twice not to leave the crate.
The crate was where he had been asked twice not to leave it.

Pilarchik moved it with his foot, got the door up, and went in, and the shop smelled the way it smelled, which was of neatsfoot oil and hot rubber and the particular dust that comes off leather when leather is cut, and which he had stopped being able to smell in the first month and could only smell now if he had been away a week.

He was twenty-five. He had the lease and the machines and fourteen dollars in the drawer from Saturday, and a mother in Pennsauken who told people her son had a business on River Road in Camden, which was true, and who said it in a way that made it sound larger than it was, which he had decided some time ago was her business and not his.
The first pair on the rack was a woman's brown pump with the heel gone at the breast, and he had it in the clamp before the door had finished swinging.

By nine the block was doing what the block did. The bakery truck went by and then the ice truck went by, and next door up the barber put his pole on, and two doors down the awning came out over the drugstore in three jerks because the crank had a flat spot in it that Cohen had been going to have seen to since before Pilarchik took the lease. You could set a watch by the crank. Three jerks and a pause and a fourth, and then the shade came down over the window with the trusses and the hot water bottles in it, and that was ten minutes past nine.
A man came in with a work boot and a story about the work boot.

The story was that he had caught the toe on a plate at the yard and the sole had come away at the front, and he wanted to know could it be done today because he was on nights. The truth, which Pilarchik could see and did not say, was that the boot was four years old and the stitching had gone all round and the plate had only finished what the last two winters had started. He could sew the toe. It would hold for a month and then it would go at the shank instead.
He said he could sew the toe.

He said it would want a dollar ten, and the man made the face that men make, and Pilarchik said that he could do it for eighty cents if the man was content to have it done the quick way, and the man thought about it and said no, do it right, and paid the dollar ten on the spot in three quarters, three dimes and a nickel, counting it out onto the glass.

That was the transaction and there was nothing in it. But there is a kind of accounting that a man in a trade keeps that is not in any book, and Pilarchik kept it, and what went into it that morning was that a man on nights at the yard had eighty cents in his pocket and had chosen to spend a dollar ten. In 1947 in East Camden that was what the difference was. Everybody had the eighty cents. What they had that was new was the other thirty.

He could feel it in the rack. The rack in 1944 had been half resoles and half nothing, and the nothing was people going without. The rack now was full at both ends, and half of it was work he had been asked to do properly rather than cheaply, and a third of it was shoes that people could have replaced and had brought to him instead because they liked them.

That last third was the part he would have had trouble explaining to his mother. A man brings you a shoe he could throw away. He brings it because his wife bought it for him, or because it fits, or because he does not want to break in another one, and he stands there while you turn it over, and he tells you where it rubs. Nobody tells a shop clerk where a shoe rubs. They tell you.

The block ran up from the corner in a way a man could hold in his head without ever having decided to learn it. Cohen had the corner, the drugstore with the awning and the flat spot in the crank, and the family over the top of it. Then the door to the upstairs rooms, which was its own door with its own bell and a strip of frosted glass in it, and which belonged to the same building and might as well have been in another town. Then a blank stretch of brick with a hoarding on it advertising a shoe polish Pilarchik did not stock and had twice been asked for. Then his own window. Then Hoover, with the pole and the two chairs and the boy. Then front steps and painted sills for a while, and then the tailor, who had the last shop before the street stopped being shops and went back to being houses.

Every one of them was let. That was the fact about 1947 that nobody standing in it thought about, because a thing that is true of every door on a street stops being a fact and becomes the weather. There had been a year, and it was not long ago, when three of those windows had been papered over from the inside and the paper had gone yellow, and the men who had had those leases had gone to the yards or the Victor or into the army, and had not come back to the leases. Now the paper was down and there was stock behind all of it and the second floors had people sleeping in them.

Pilarchik had come in at the good end of that. He knew it in the way you know a thing you have not earned, which is to say pleasantly and without much examination. A man who opens a shoe repair in 1943 is a man taking a risk with his mother's money. A man who opens one in 1946 is a man who can hardly help himself.

At half past ten the barber's boy came over with two chairs' worth of gossip and a heel lift to be cut, and Pilarchik cut the lift while the boy talked, and what the boy said was that the Klingman girl was engaged and that a fellow on Thirty-first had bought a Studebaker, an actual Studebaker, off the lot, and that the man in the second floor over the drugstore had been in the chair on Saturday and had sat the whole time without saying anything at all, which the boy thought was a peculiar way to be and which Hoover apparently had not thought was anything.
Pilarchik said that some men did not care to talk in a chair.
The boy said that everybody talked in a chair. That was what a chair was for.
Pilarchik gave him the lift and told him to tell Hoover it was the last one out of that hide and he would want to know before he promised anybody else a brown.

At noon he ate a sandwich standing at the bench because sitting down at noon was a thing that led to sitting down at two, and while he was standing there the second floor over the drugstore went past the window on the far side of the street, going up toward Thirty-second, walking the way he always walked, which was quickly and with his shoulders set, and carrying nothing.

Pilarchik registered him for slightly less than a second, in the way that a man in a shop registers everything that moves past his window, and the entire content of the registration was: him, going up.

He had cut a strap for the mother in the spring. She had come in with a shopping bag with a broken handle, not a shoe at all, and had been apologetic about it, and he had riveted a strap on it in about four minutes and had not charged her, and she had been so grateful about it that it had been slightly uncomfortable for both of them. She worked at a soap plant. She had a way of standing at a counter with her purse held in front of her in both hands, like a woman waiting to be told something she already knew.
That was the extent of what he had. Four years on the block, a woman with a shopping bag, and a son who went past the window quickly.

In the afternoon a girl came in with white sandals that had been dyed once already and wanted them dyed navy, and Pilarchik told her the truth, which was that they had been dyed once already and would come out uneven and she would be disappointed, and she said do it anyway, and he did it anyway, and they came out uneven, and she was delighted with them.

He put them in tissue for her. He was not a man who put things in tissue. He did it because she was pleased with something he had told her she would not be pleased with, and because it was August, and because the drawer had fourteen dollars in it and had gone all week without going under nine.
At six he swept, and cashed up, and pulled the shade, and stood a moment in the doorway with the key in his hand.

The block at six on an August evening had a smell that came off the pavement and off the trolley wire and off the back of the bakery, all at once, and there were kids on the step at the grocer's and a woman calling one of them in, and further up somebody was practising a bugle very badly, three notes and then the same three notes, going up and stopping in the same place every time and starting again.
Pilarchik locked the door.
He thought, walking to the corner for the bus, that he would be able to take the lease on the whole of the ground floor within two years if the trade held.
The trade held.
1. Aug 4. 3208. did not say good morning.

The bugle had come out of a closing-down sale at a place on Federal that had sold band instruments and sheet music and, latterly, radios, and it had cost his father four dollars and had come with a mute that did not fit it and a booklet with a boy on the cover standing in a posture no boy has ever stood in.

He was ten. He had wanted a bugle for about sixteen days, which at ten is a considerable stretch of wanting, and the sixteen days had been spent on a campaign of a kind he was already good at, which consisted of not mentioning it very often and being extremely reasonable when he did.

His father had come up the stairs with it on a Tuesday in July, in the paper, under his arm, and had put it on the kitchen table and said that it was not a toy and that there would be no playing of it in the store.
There had been no playing of it in the store.
There had been playing of it more or less everywhere else.

The apartment sat over the drugstore on the corner, and you got to it by the second door, the one with the frosted panel, and up a straight run of thirteen stairs that turned once at the top onto a landing with a window at the far end that looked out over the back. The landing was the part of the house he liked best, for the reason that it was nobody's. The kitchen was his mother's and the front room was for company and his grandmother's room was his grandmother's in a way that was not open for discussion, but the landing was simply a place with a floor, and he could lie on it on his stomach with his chin on his hands and be out of everybody's way for an hour at a time.

The window at the end of the landing was the other reason. It was a sash with a deep sill, and it looked over the back of the block, which from the second floor was a different country from the front. The front was awnings and people going somewhere. The back was forty feet of yard behind every house, and hedges that had given up, and board fences at three or four different angles built by three or four different men with three or four different ideas about where the line was, and a grape arbour, and on a Monday the lines of washing the whole length of it like flags on a ship.
Directly under the landing window there was a flat piece of roof over the back part of the store where the stock came in. It was tarred, with a low parapet, and he was not allowed on it.
He had been on it twice.

The second time his mother had seen him from the yard and had not shouted, which was worse, and he had come in over the sill and along the landing and stood in the kitchen and been talked to at some length about the words flat roof, and about what a flat roof is for and what it is not for. He had agreed with all of it. He had privately retained the view that a flat roof with a parapet on it and the tar still warm at seven in the evening is one of the better places a person can be, and that this was simply a thing you could not put to an adult.

His own room was the second door on the left off the landing, and it had a window on the street, and a bed, and a chest, and a closet that was deeper than it looked because the house was old and had been divided oddly, so that the closet went back about four feet and then turned a little to the left and had a shelf at the end of the turn that you could not see from the doorway.
The bugle lived on that shelf, in its paper.

He kept it there partly because his mother had said to keep it somewhere and partly because getting it out involved going in past the coats and around the turn and reaching up, which was a small ceremony, and he was at an age where a small ceremony improved a thing.

Downstairs the store was doing what a drugstore does at six in the evening in September, which is not much and steadily. He could hear it through the floor as a general sound with occasional edges on it: the screen door, the register, the particular carrying tone his father used for the fountain end that was not the tone he used at the prescription counter. His grandmother had come down at four, as she did, and had sat on the stool by the cigar case with her ankles crossed and had told two people that her son was a doctor of pharmacy, which was true and which she said as though it were being contested.

The store itself he knew the way you know a room you are not the point of. There was a fountain at the near end with eight stools and a marble counter that stayed cold in August, and the cigar case, and the rack of magazines his grandmother squared up whenever she passed it, and then the long middle with the shelves, and then the back where the counter came up higher and his father worked and where a boy did not go behind. It smelled of three things at once and he could not have named any of them.
At half past six his mother called up the stairs that if he was going to do it he should do it before supper and not after, and he said all right, and got the bugle off the shelf.
He took it to his room because his room had the street window and the street window was the point.

There is a thing that happens with a brass instrument and a boy which is that the instrument is louder than the boy has any conception of, and that the boy finds this out, and that after he has found it out he goes on anyway. He had got three notes. They were the first three of the call that begins the way that call begins, and he could get all three of them cleanly about one time in four, and the other three times the third one went somewhere it had no business going and came out as a sort of animal.
He played the three notes.
He waited.
He played the three notes.

The window was open because it was the second week of September and still warm enough at night to want it open, and there was no reason on earth to close a window in September in Camden, and so the three notes went out of it and down the street and along the fronts of the shops and up over the back lots and off the wall of the brewery two blocks over, which he did not know about but which was the reason the sound came back to him a half-beat late and sounding like somebody else.

He got the third note. He got it four times running, which he had never done, and he stopped and stood there in the middle of the room with the thing in both hands, and the feeling that went through him was one he would have been unable to describe and that did not need describing.
Then he got it wrong six times.
At about ten past seven the window across the way went up and a woman leaned out and shouted, in a voice of real warmth, that he was getting there.
He shouted back thank you.

She said her brother had played one in the Legion band and it had taken him two years to get past exactly where the boy was now, and that he was to keep at it, and that if he could get the whole call by Christmas she would give him a quarter.
This was a serious offer and he took it seriously.

Around the block the same three notes had by now been heard for about nine weeks by perhaps forty households, and the settled opinion of the street, insofar as a street has one, was that it was a nice thing for a boy to be doing and that it was better than a great many of the alternatives. The man at the grocer's had asked him once whether he could play anything that a person could dance to. The barber, when he cut his hair, had told him that a bugle was the only instrument that had ever won a war, which was the sort of thing the barber said. Nobody had complained. It would not have occurred to anybody to complain. It was a boy with a horn in the evening in a street where everybody's windows were open and somebody's radio was always on and there were nineteen children on the block under the age of twelve.

At twenty past seven his mother came up and stood in his doorway with a dish towel and said that was enough now and to close the window because the smell of the cabbage was going out and the smell of everybody else's supper was coming in.
He closed the window.

That was the whole of it. He put the bugle back in its paper and carried it around the turn in the closet and up onto the shelf, and the sound of the three notes stopped existing on the street and existed only in the building, where it had been going all along anyway, up through the joists and along the joists and out at the other end the way sound does in an old house that has been divided oddly, and where nobody had ever mentioned it, because nobody mentions the sounds a building makes.
Supper was liver, which he did not like, and potatoes, which he did.

His father came up at a quarter to eight with the register tape in his shirt pocket and washed his hands for a long time at the kitchen sink, the way he did, and sat down and said that a man had come in that afternoon and asked for something for a headache and had described the headache for twelve minutes.
His grandmother said that was what people wanted, somebody to describe it to.
His father said that was very likely true and that he wished they would describe it to somebody with a stool.

They ate. Afterward his father asked him how many notes he was up to now and he said three, and his father said that when he got to five there was a thing he would show him about how to hold his mouth, and the boy asked what thing, and his father said that it was a thing you could not explain, only show, and that it would keep until five.
It was fully dark by half past eight, which it had not been a month ago, and that was the only thing about September that he had anything against.
He lay on the landing for a while with his chin on his hands.
